claims.text: Controlled pre-oxidation of boron-rich Fe–B components will significantly improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion relative to untreated surfaces.
Heating Fe–B components in a controlled oxygen atmosphere at 800–850°C for 1–2 hours will form an adherent, nanocrystalline Al2O3 surface scale.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will be dense and well integrated with the boride-based substrate.
Al2O3 is chemically inert under the proposed molten-aluminum service conditions.
Al2O3 has a high melting point.
The pre-formed Al2O3 layer will act as a physical and chemical barrier between the Fe–B substrate and molten aluminum.
The Al2O3 layer will impede dissolution of the Fe–B substrate in molten aluminum.
The Al2O3 layer will impede reactive wetting of the substrate by molten aluminum.
Impeded dissolution and reactive wetting will reduce the rate of corrosive attack during hot-dip aluminum plating.
Untreated boride-based Fe–B components typically undergo rapid corrosion and degradation in molten aluminum.
Pre-oxidized components will have a significantly slower corrosion rate than untreated components during exposure to molten aluminum at 700–750°C.
Pre-oxidized components will retain mechanical integrity better than untreated components during molten-aluminum exposure.
The corrosion-resistance improvement will persist under continuous molten-aluminum service at 700–750°C following pre-oxidation at 800–850°C.
Substantially higher operating temperatures or mechanical stresses may compromise oxide-scale adhesion or integrity.
The Al2O3-barrier mechanism is well established in high-temperature environments.

contradictions.description: The stated starting material is an Fe–B alloy with no pre-formed oxide, yet treatment with oxygen alone is asserted to produce Al2O3 before molten-aluminum exposure. No aluminum-bearing constituent, coating, or other aluminum source is specified, leaving the proposed mediator composition internally unexplained.
